variants.title: Run the connected lifecycle
variants.context: The lesson runs one connected lifecycle: frame and baseline, build trustworthy evidence, train and gate candidates, release with containment, then observe outcomes and adapt.
variants.prompt: A payments team is designing a fraud decision service. Put the lifecycle stages in order.

items.text: Compare candidates with that baseline over representative time periods, slices, calibration, robustness, and resource use.
Release behind shadow traffic, a canary, immutable artifacts, and predeclared automatic rollback conditions.
Name the consumer, the target, the cost of a wrong decline against a wrong approval, and the rules baseline to beat.
Version the sources and feature logic, enforce point in time correctness, and keep lineage from raw event to training row.
Join predictions, decisions, exposures, and delayed chargebacks, watch for drift, and retrain only from validated evidence.

variants.hint: Which stage decides what every later stage is even measuring?
variants.explanation: Frame, evidence, gate, contain, observe. The baseline and error costs are chosen first because they define what the later stages have to prove.

variants.title: Run the connected lifecycle
variants.context: The lesson runs one connected lifecycle: frame and baseline, build trustworthy evidence, train and gate candidates, release with containment, then observe outcomes and adapt.
variants.prompt: A team is designing the ranking system behind a home feed. Put the lifecycle stages in order.

items.text: Pin the event sources and feature definitions so a training row can only see what existed at request time.
Roll out to a small cohort with fallbacks and immutable artifacts while the previous ranker stays deployable.
Write down who consumes the ranking, what a good session looks like, and the popularity baseline the model must beat.
Log exposure beside every prediction so later engagement can be attributed to the policy that produced it.
Gate candidates on held out weeks, slice quality, calibration, latency, and cost per prediction.

variants.hint: Point in time correctness belongs to a stage that runs before any candidate is trained.
variants.explanation: Evidence has to be trustworthy before training, and exposure logging has to exist before outcomes can teach the next model.

variants.title: Run the connected lifecycle
variants.context: The lesson runs one connected lifecycle: frame and baseline, build trustworthy evidence, train and gate candidates, release with containment, then observe outcomes and adapt.
variants.prompt: A support team wants a model to route new tickets to a queue. Put the lifecycle stages in order.

items.text: Assemble evidence with lineage: ticket text, account facts, and the versions of each at submission time.
Deploy with containment: shadow first, then a canary that rolls back automatically if reassignment rate rises.
Observe resolutions and reassignments, then retrain only after the joined evidence has been validated.
Train candidates and gate them against the current keyword router on recent weeks and on the rarest queues.
Define the decision: which queue receives the ticket, and what a wrong route costs the customer.

variants.hint: The rarest queues matter at the stage where candidates are compared, not later.
variants.explanation: The same five stages hold for a routing model, and the containment stage exists so the first real exposure is bounded and reversible.

variants.title: Earn authority step by step
variants.context: Promotion needs progressively stronger evidence and bounded exposure: replay offline against the current baseline, run in shadow with no authority, canary with bounded authority, then promote or roll back on predeclared checks.
variants.prompt: A candidate model is ready for release. Put the promotion steps in order.

items.text: Increase traffic only when the predeclared checks pass, keeping the previous artifact and routing policy ready to restore.
Replay it against a time based holdout, critical slices, calibration, robustness, latency, and cost beside the production baseline.
Run it on production inputs without affecting decisions, comparing feature parity, outputs, latency, and resource demand.
Expose a small representative cohort with guardrails for quality, latency, errors, safety, and business harm.

variants.hint: Each step buys the candidate more authority than the one before it.
variants.explanation: Offline evidence cannot reproduce every production dependency, so exposure grows only as the evidence gets stronger.

variants.title: Earn authority step by step
variants.context: Promotion needs progressively stronger evidence and bounded exposure: replay offline against the current baseline, run in shadow with no authority, canary with bounded authority, then promote or roll back on predeclared checks.
variants.prompt: A candidate looks strong offline but fails later. Put what happened in order.

items.text: Routing restores the previous artifact, which was never deleted at promotion time.
Offline replay shows a small lift on the time based holdout with no slice regression.
Shadow traffic confirms feature parity but reveals a p99 higher than the baseline under real load.
The canary cohort crosses the latency guardrail and fallback use climbs with it.

variants.hint: Real load shows up before user impact does, if the steps are run in order.
variants.explanation: Rollback is a system capability rather than a reconstruction exercise, which is why the previous artifact stays deployable.

variants.title: Earn authority step by step
variants.context: Promotion needs progressively stronger evidence and bounded exposure: replay offline against the current baseline, run in shadow with no authority, canary with bounded authority, then promote or roll back on predeclared checks.
variants.prompt: A model retrained after concept drift is going out. Put the promotion steps in order.

items.text: Promote it while keeping the previous bundle deployable rather than rebuilding it later.
Replay the retrained candidate on the most recent weeks and on the slices that drifted.
Give it a bounded cohort with rollback conditions written before the cohort is opened.
Shadow it against live traffic to confirm the feature values it sees match what training saw.

variants.hint: A retrained model has no more earned authority than a new one.
variants.explanation: Fresh training data does not shorten the path, because the evidence each step produces is about production behavior, not about the training run.

variants.title: Size the serving path
variants.context: Serving capacity and latency are part of the design contract. Size the path from peak traffic rather than averages, and spend the request budget across bounded feature lookup and inference.
variants.prompt: A request time model server sustains 420 predictions per second per replica. The fraud path averages 900 requests per second and peaks at 1800. How many replicas are needed to cover the peak?
variants.hint: Percentiles and peak traffic decide capacity, and a partial replica cannot serve requests.
variants.explanation: Peak 1800 divided by 420 per replica is 4.29, and capacity has to be rounded up, so 5 replicas cover the peak.

mistakes.feedback: That rounds 4.29 replicas down and leaves part of the peak unserved.
That sizes from the 900 average rather than from the peak the contract has to survive.

variants.title: Size the serving path
variants.context: Serving capacity and latency are part of the design contract. Size the path from peak traffic rather than averages, and spend the request budget across bounded feature lookup and inference.
variants.prompt: The product gives the decision service a 120 ms budget end to end. A bounded feature lookup takes 39 ms and the model call takes 58 ms at p99. How many milliseconds are left for everything else before the deadline?
variants.hint: The budget is spent by every hop on the path, not only by inference.
variants.explanation: 39 ms plus 58 ms is 97 ms of the 120 ms budget, so 23 ms remain for serialization, network, and policy before the deadline.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts only the feature lookup and ignores the model call.
That reports the time already spent rather than the headroom that is left.

variants.title: Size the serving path
variants.context: Serving capacity and latency are part of the design contract. Size the path from peak traffic rather than averages, and spend the request budget across bounded feature lookup and inference.
variants.prompt: A scheduled batch scorer must score 18 million entities inside a 5 hour window. How many predictions per second must it sustain on average?
variants.hint: Convert the window into the same units as the rate you are asked for.
variants.explanation: 5 hours is 18000 seconds, and 18 million divided by 18000 is 1000 predictions per second.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by 5 hours rather than by the seconds in those hours.
That divides by 300 minutes, which gives a per minute rate instead.

variants.title: Choose the inference pattern
variants.context: Scheduled batch precomputes on a schedule when predictions that are minutes or hours old are acceptable. Request time online spends the request latency and availability budget to use live context. Hybrid precomputes expensive candidates and then filters or reranks online.
variants.prompt: A fraud decision must return while the card authorization is waiting, and it depends on counters that changed seconds ago. Which pattern is the right starting point?
options: Request time online inference, with a bounded feature lookup and an explicit timeout policy.
Scheduled batch scoring, with the stored score looked up during the authorization.
Hybrid retrieval and rerank, precomputing candidates and reranking them at request time.
optionFeedback: Correct. The decision needs live context inside the request, so the model runs on the critical path with a documented fallback.
Wrong. A stored score cannot see counters that moved seconds ago, which is exactly the evidence this decision needs.
Wrong. There is no large candidate set to precompute here, so the extra path adds operations without buying freshness.
variants.hint: Ask what evidence has to be fresh at the instant the decision is made.
variants.explanation: Online inference is chosen when the product needs live context, and it is paid for out of the request latency and availability budget.

variants.title: Choose the inference pattern
variants.context: Scheduled batch precomputes on a schedule when predictions that are minutes or hours old are acceptable. Request time online spends the request latency and availability budget to use live context. Hybrid precomputes expensive candidates and then filters or reranks online.
variants.prompt: A home feed must rank millions of candidate items against session context that is seconds old, at 6500 requests per second. Which pattern fits?
options: Request time online inference that scores the full candidate set for every request.
Hybrid: precompute the expensive candidate set, then filter and rerank with fresh context online.
Scheduled batch scoring of the whole feed for every user a few times each day.
optionFeedback: Wrong. Scoring millions of candidates inside the request cannot meet the latency budget at this traffic.
Correct. Scale is precomputed and freshness is applied online, which is the case that justifies two clocks.
Wrong. A feed rebuilt a few times a day cannot use context that arrived seconds before the request.
variants.hint: Both scale and freshness are binding here, not just one of them.
variants.explanation: Hybrid earns its extra operational cost only when the workload demands precomputed scale and fresh context at the same time.

variants.title: Choose the inference pattern
variants.context: Scheduled batch precomputes on a schedule when predictions that are minutes or hours old are acceptable. Request time online spends the request latency and availability budget to use live context. Hybrid precomputes expensive candidates and then filters or reranks online.
variants.prompt: A warehouse restock forecast covers 40 million item and store pairs, is regenerated weekly, and planners read it from a table. Which pattern fits?
options: Scheduled batch scoring that writes the forecasts to a prediction store planners read.
Request time online inference so each planner view reflects the newest available signal.
Hybrid: precompute candidate forecasts and rerank them when a planner opens the table.
optionFeedback: Correct. Predictions that are hours or days old are acceptable, so precomputing is the simplest sufficient design.
Wrong. Nothing in the workflow needs live context, so this spends latency and availability budget for no product gain.
Wrong. There is no second clock to serve here, so the added path is complexity the freshness need does not justify.
variants.hint: Start from the freshness the product actually accepts.
variants.explanation: The strongest design is the smallest system that satisfies the decision contract, and batch is sufficient when staleness costs nothing.

variants.title: Diagnose the failing part of the loop
variants.context: Production failures live in different parts of the loop. Input health, prediction health, service health, outcome health, and learning health point at different responses, so treating every alert as retrain the model can make the incident worse.
variants.prompt: Right after a feature release, training and serving parity checks disagree on a 30 day purchase counter and scores shift within the hour. Service health and label delay are unchanged. What is the first response?
options: Add capacity to the feature service and raise its timeout so the counter is computed in time.
Restore the previous bundle and fix the definition so serving matches what the model was evaluated with.
Retrain the model on the newest data so that it learns the meaning the feature now has online.
optionFeedback: Wrong. Nothing points at saturation here, so capacity work leaves the mismatched semantics in place.
Correct. The deployed model must receive features with the meaning, units, time boundary, and version it was evaluated with.
Wrong. Retraining bakes an unreviewed definition change into the model and hides the broken contract instead of repairing it.
variants.hint: The alert is about meaning, not about volume or freshness.
variants.explanation: Reusing a feature name is not compatibility, so the fix restores the evaluated contract before any retraining is considered.

variants.title: Diagnose the failing part of the loop
variants.context: Production failures live in different parts of the loop. Input health, prediction health, service health, outcome health, and learning health point at different responses, so treating every alert as retrain the model can make the incident worse.
variants.prompt: Prediction volume is normal and quality metrics look flat, but outcome join coverage falls after a new surface ships without exposure identifiers. What should happen before the next retraining run?
options: Shorten the join window until coverage returns to the number the dashboard used to show.
Restore exposure logging on that surface, because partial joins teach the next model the current blind spot.
Retrain now on the joined rows that did arrive, since those outcomes are still real.
optionFeedback: Wrong. Changing the window hides the gap in the metric without recovering any missing evidence.
Correct. Learning health has to be repaired first, since exposure identifiers are what make outcomes attributable.
Wrong. The rows that joined are the ones the current policy already exposed, so training on them reinforces that policy.
variants.hint: Ask what a missing identifier does to the next training set, not to today's dashboard.
variants.explanation: Predictions influence which outcomes ever arrive, so exposure logging is repaired before joined evidence is used for retraining.

variants.title: Diagnose the failing part of the loop
variants.context: Production failures live in different parts of the loop. Input health, prediction health, service health, outcome health, and learning health point at different responses, so treating every alert as retrain the model can make the incident worse.
variants.prompt: Schemas validate, feature age is normal, and p99 latency is flat, but delayed quality and calibration have decayed slowly over six weeks. What does the loop need?
options: A rollback to the previous model bundle, which served the earlier population well.
More serving capacity, because slow quality decay usually follows creeping saturation.
Fresh validated labels and a retrained candidate, gated the usual way, since the relationship moved.
optionFeedback: Wrong. The earlier bundle learned the same outdated relationship, so restoring it does not recover quality.
Wrong. Latency and feature age are healthy, which rules saturation out as the explanation here.
Correct. Gradual concept drift is a learning problem, and it is answered with fresh labels and a gated retrain.
variants.hint: Input and service health are both clean, so which health signal is left?
variants.explanation: Concept drift changes the relationship between features and outcomes, so it needs new evidence rather than a restore or more capacity.
